newsitem.title: UK: International action needed against Burma - Britain.
newsitem.headline: International action needed against Burma - Britain.

text.p: Britain said on Monday fresh international action was needed against the Burmese government after it stopped opposition leader and Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi from delivering a weekend speech.

"The UK believes it will be necessary to take further international action against the SLORC (Burma's ruling army council). We will be proposing possible measures to European Union partners," the Foreign Office said in a statement.

A Foreign Office source said Britain, the former colonial power in Burma, would raise the subject of possible action at a meeting of senior officials of the 15 EU member states in Brussels on Tuesday.

He declined to speculate on precisely what Britain would propose. Checkpoints were set up on all roads leading to Suu Kyi's Rangoon residence early on Friday to prevent a three-day congress of her National League for Democracy being held there.
A spokesman for the SLORC, the State Law and Order Council, has said 109 people are being detained in government guest houses.

Japan, Burma's biggest aid donor, earlier expressed concern at the developments, with government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama telling a news conference: "The freedom of political parties to conduct their activities must be recognised."

Japan suspended some big aid projects after bloody crackdowns on pro-democracy forces in 1988 but has held off from using its aid of about $140 million a year as a lever to ensure the country moves towards democracy."

"We deplore SLORC actions preventing Aung San Suu Kyi from delivering her weekend speech: restrictions on freedom of speech and assembly are a breach of basic human rights," the Foreign Office statement said.
It said Britain's ambassador in Rangoon had been asked to raise the matter with the government.

EU member Denmark has been pressing for sanctions against Burma since its unaccredited honorary consul in Rangoon, James Leander Nichols, who was godfather to Suu Kyi, died in June in what it says were suspicious circumstances.

Nichols, who also represented EU member Finland and non-members Norway and Switzerland, was arrested in April and sentenced to three years in prison for operating home telephones and fax machines without permission.
Britain has in the past opposed sanctions unless they can be agreed at the United Nations, but earlier this year cancelled a trade mission to Rangoon.
